parts.what: Two licensed super-premium international brands sold in India; management describes them as a 'stellar' double-digit growth and profit engine, with wide accessory ranges (watches, kidswear, innerwear, small leather goods) making up roughly 20% of their retail business.

parts.name: Arrow
parts.what: A formal/premium menswear brand (with a premium '1851' line and wrinkle-free shirts) that reached a better stage of profitability in FY25, but was subdued in Q4 FY26 on a model change and weak wedding season; it is described as sitting mainly in the wholesale business.

parts.name: Flying Machine
parts.what: A youth denim brand, now fully owned after buying the residual stake, repositioned as a unisex, on-trend Gen Z denim brand — it grew over 10% in Q4 FY26 with double-digit retail like-for-like and 70% online B2C growth, and gets a dedicated dotcom in H2 FY27.

parts.name: Retail / EBO (exclusive brand outlets)
parts.what: The company's own branded stores — the single biggest channel at roughly INR 2,000 crores in FY25, growing via ~1.2–1.4 lakh sq ft of net new space a year, 50 stores added in Q4 FY26 alone, and like-for-like growth of about 8% in FY26 and 11.6% in Q1 FY27.

parts.name: Online B2C (direct-to-consumer online)
parts.what: Sales through the company's own brand websites/apps plus omni and marketplace tie-ups, the fastest-growing channel at 38–40% growth, rising from 11% to 14% of revenue in FY26 and 18% by Q1 FY27, deliberately replacing lower-margin online B2B.

parts.name: Wholesale / MBO / department stores (including online B2B)
parts.what: Selling to multi-brand outlets, department stores and online partners rather than end consumers — still delivering strong double-digit secondary sales growth, but shrinking as a share as management pivots toward direct channels (direct is now 62% of sales).

parts.name: Adjacent categories
parts.what: Non-core-apparel lines — footwear, innerwear, accessories, watches, kidswear, small leather goods — that management now reports as about 24% of total business and a designated growth driver, growing around 20% in FY25.

parts.name: Sephora (divested)
parts.what: A beauty retail business sold to Reliance Retail after Q2 FY24 at an enterprise value of INR 216 crores, which management called the completion of its portfolio rationalization, with proceeds used to retire debt and focus on the five remaining brands.

overview.what_it_does: Ashapura Minechem is an Indian mining and minerals company that digs up rocks and either ships them out raw or processes them into higher-value industrial materials. Its biggest business by far is in Guinea, West Africa, where it holds mining concessions for bauxite (the ore used to make aluminium) and iron ore, and exports bauxite by sea, mainly to Chinese alumina refineries — it shipped about 8 million tons in FY26 versus 3.5 million the year before, and built its own roads and three ports to do it. Its older, smaller India business mines bentonite clay and other minerals in Gujarat and converts them into value-added products such as bleaching clay, kaolin, organoclay and ceramic materials, sold into edible oils, foundries, oil and gas, paints, construction and other industries and exported to more than 80 countries. In FY26 the group did INR 5,237 crores of revenue with INR 674 crores of EBITDA, of which Guinea supplied roughly INR 4,200 crores of revenue and INR 561 crores of EBITDA — so the company is essentially a bauxite exporter with a specialty-minerals arm attached.

parts.name: Guinea operations (bauxite)
parts.what: Mines bauxite from three concessions holding over 700 million tons of reserves and ships it to customers (priced around $70/ton CIF China, roughly $10.5 per ton of EBITDA in Q3 FY26); it is the dominant part of the group, about 76% of Q3 FY26 revenue and about INR 4,200 crores of FY26 revenue, with port capacity being expanded from 15 to 20 million tons and a long-term volume target of 15 million tons by FY27-28.

parts.name: Guinea iron ore
parts.what: A licensed iron ore resource of over 300 million tons that is currently only sold locally to a nearby beneficiation plant after trial supplies; management calls it small today but expects meaningful volumes and is studying building its own beneficiation plant within three to four quarters.

parts.name: Bentonite & Allied Minerals and White Performance Minerals
parts.what: The core India vertical, mining and processing bentonite (700,000 tons capacity, largest in India and third largest globally) and kaolin into industrial products for foundries, detergents, animal feed, oil and gas and construction; together with the white minerals it generated about INR 998 crores of revenue and INR 112 crores of EBITDA in FY26, and is the main target of a planned INR 150 crores of India capex.

parts.name: Specialty Adsorbent Solutions (Ashapura Perfoclay Limited, 50% JV)
parts.what: Makes bleaching clay — a bentonite derivative used to purify edible oils, turning a roughly $40/ton raw mineral into a $400/ton product — from what management calls the world's largest single-location plant at 200,000 tons; it contributed positively in FY26 but was hurt by a sharp rise in sulfuric acid, its key raw material.

parts.name: Advanced Ceramic Materials (stake in Orient Ceratech Limited)
parts.what: Produces industrial ceramic materials including proppants from what the company says is the first plant of its kind in India; it is a smaller contributor but was the India segment's bright spot, delivering encouraging growth versus the prior year.

overview.what_it_does: Ashoka Buildcon is an Indian construction contractor, based in Nashik, Maharashtra, that builds infrastructure for government bodies — mainly highways and roads, but also railway systems, power transmission and distribution networks, buildings and urban works like bridges and flyovers. Most of its money comes from fixed-price EPC (engineering, procurement and construction) contracts won from clients such as NHAI, state road and public works departments, the Mumbai municipal corporation (BMC), CIDCO and Indian Railways, where it is paid to build and books revenue as work progresses; its balance order book was about INR 15,312 crores at March 2026, with standalone income of INR 5,952 crores in FY26. Separately, it also owns and operates road assets itself — collecting tolls from motorists on the Jaora-Nayagaon toll road (about INR 77 crores a quarter) and receiving fixed semi-annual 'annuity' payments from NHAI on hybrid annuity (HAM) projects — and periodically sells these completed road companies to infrastructure funds (KKR, NIIF, Maple Infrastructure Trust) for lump-sum proceeds it uses to cut debt. Almost all work is in India, with a growing overseas EPC business in Saudi Arabia, Angola, Liberia and Guyana.

parts.name: Road EPC (highways)
parts.what: Builds and widens national and state highways under plain construction contracts where the government pays the full cost — the single biggest business, at roughly half of quarterly revenue and, together with railways, about 66% of the order book.

parts.name: HAM road projects (hybrid annuity)
parts.what: Builds NHAI highways through separate project companies (SPVs) in which Ashoka puts up part of the equity, then earns fixed annuity payments from NHAI once complete — about INR 1,619 crores of the order book at March 2026, and the assets it most often sells on to investors.

parts.name: BOT toll roads
parts.what: Owns road concessions where it keeps the toll money collected from traffic; after selling most of its portfolio, this is now essentially the Jaora-Nayagaon toll road, bringing in roughly INR 77 crores of gross toll per quarter.

parts.name: Power T&D EPC
parts.what: Builds electricity transmission and distribution networks, including overseas (Angola) — the second-largest line, at about 30% of the order book and roughly a fifth of revenue.

parts.name: Railways EPC
parts.what: Executes railway works such as signalling and anti-collision systems — a smaller line at around INR 1,420 crores of order book and about 8-10% of revenue.

parts.name: Building and urban infrastructure EPC
parts.what: Constructs buildings, bridges, flyovers and airport-linked structures (for example BMC's Mithi River works, a Navi Mumbai airport bridge, a Daman signature bridge) — the smallest named segment at roughly 3-4% of the order book, though large recent wins are lifting it.

parts.name: International EPC
parts.what: A growing overseas arm doing roads and power distribution in Guyana, Liberia, Angola and a hotel package in Saudi Arabia's Diriyah project (Ashoka's share INR 900 crores) — described by management as a strategic expansion rather than a core earnings driver yet.

parts.name: Asset monetization
parts.what: Not an operating business but a recurring source of cash: selling completed road SPVs and other holdings (10 HAM and BOT projects sold in FY26 alone, including INR 1,814 crores from five BOT SPVs) to cut consolidated debt, which fell from INR 4,910 crores to about INR 2,778 crores.

parts.name: City gas distribution (exited)
parts.what: Formerly held a 51% stake in Unison Enviro, a piped-gas business, sold to Mahanagar Gas in FY24 for INR 286.67 crores to Ashoka — no longer part of the company.

overview.what_it_does: Ashok Leyland is an Indian commercial-vehicle maker: it builds and sells trucks and buses — from small 2-4 tonne pickups and mini-trucks up to heavy haulage trucks, tippers, tractor-trailers and city/intercity buses — plus the diesel engines, spare parts and defence vehicles that go with them. Its customers are fleet owners, individual truck operators, state transport bodies and bus fleets, industrial engine buyers, government defence buyers and overseas distributors. It makes money mainly by manufacturing and selling vehicles through a dealer and service network (2,104 touch points at end-FY26) and by selling higher-margin spare parts, service and engines afterwards; the calls stress premium products, cost savings and better price realisation as the profit levers. It sells mostly in India, with export 'home markets' in the Gulf (GCC), Africa and SAARC and a push into ASEAN and Europe; FY26 revenue was about INR 44,007 crores with a 13% EBITDA margin and INR 3,914 crores of profit before exceptional items.

parts.name: MHCV (medium & heavy commercial vehicles) — trucks
parts.what: The core business: heavy trucks, tippers, tractor-trailers and multi-axle vehicles (AVTR, HIPPO, TAURUS ranges), selling 105,905 units in FY26 at roughly a 30% domestic market share, with a stated medium-term goal of 35%.

parts.name: MHCV — buses
parts.what: Medium and heavy buses for state transport and private operators, where the company says it is the market leader with a 34.1% share and 20,840 units in FY26, and is expanding bus body-building capacity toward 20,000 units a year.

parts.name: LCV (light commercial vehicles)
parts.what: Smaller goods carriers like Dost, Bada Dost, Saathi and the export-focused Phoenix in the 2-4 tonne space; FY26 volume was a record 74,322 units at a 12.7% VAHAN market share, and management calls it a key growth and market-share-gain area.

parts.name: Exports / international operations (IO)
parts.what: Sales of India-built and export-specific vehicles through distributors in the GCC, Africa and SAARC — its three 'home markets' outside India — reaching a record 18,082 units in FY26, up 18.5%, with ASEAN being built as a fourth home market.

parts.name: Aftermarket / spare parts and service
parts.what: Selling spare parts and servicing vehicles through the dealer network; a steady non-vehicle revenue stream that grew about 9.5% in FY26 and is one of the 'non-CV' businesses management wants to grow substantially.

parts.name: Power Solutions (engines)
parts.what: Sells diesel and other engines for non-vehicle uses such as gensets and industrial applications; revenue grew 16.4% in FY26 and 45% year-on-year in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Defence
parts.what: Supplies vehicles to defence customers, including through subsidiary ALDS; revenue rose about 20% in FY26 (84% in Q3), with management repeatedly describing the order book and tender pipeline as strong.

parts.name: Switch Mobility (EV subsidiary)
parts.what: Makes electric buses and electric light commercial vehicles in India (and the E1 bus for Europe); it delivered 1,530 e-buses and 1,600 e-LCVs in FY26, claims leadership in both segments, turned net profitable, and had a 1,600-unit order book.

parts.name: OHM Mobility (e-MaaS subsidiary)
parts.what: Operates electric buses as a service for city and GCC transport contracts rather than selling them outright, running a fleet of over 1,400 e-buses at healthy double-digit project returns.

parts.name: Hinduja Leyland Finance and Hinduja Housing Finance
parts.what: Lending subsidiaries — HLF finances vehicle buyers (AUM about INR 59,000 crores, PAT INR 491 crores in FY26) and HHF does housing loans (AUM about INR 16,000 crores) — which both add profit and help customers buy Ashok Leyland's trucks; HLF is being reverse-merged into listed NDL Ventures to unlock value.

overview.what_it_does: Asian Paints has been in business since 1942 and describes its purpose as beautifying, preserving and transforming spaces and objects. Its core business is making and selling paints and coatings in India — decorative paint for homes across economy, premium and luxury price ranges, plus fast-growing adjacent products like waterproofing, construction chemicals and adhesives — sold mainly through a retail dealer network that management says had crossed about 1.63 lakh retail points, three to four times any competitor. It earns money by selling volume through that network at rising realisations (price increases and a richer product mix), and by adding higher-margin new products, which management says are roughly 11-12% of the top line. Alongside the core paints business it runs a B2B/Projects arm selling to builders, factories, government infrastructure and hospitality, a home décor business (kitchens, bath, lighting, UPVC windows, rugs, décor stores), industrial coatings joint ventures with PPG of the U.S., and an international business spanning Asia, the Middle East, Africa and the South Pacific.

parts.name: Decorative paints (India)
parts.what: The main business — interior and exterior wall paints, enamels and specialty finishes sold across Economy, Premium and Luxury ranges through dealers; management says the Economy end is still about 70% of the market and that Asian Paints claims a strong share in all three tiers.

parts.name: Waterproofing and construction chemicals (SmartCare / Damp Proof)
parts.what: Products that stop damp and protect buildings — from foundation admixtures to membranes, repair chemicals and topcoats, over 280 products developed in-house — described as growing at exponential rates, number one in the retail waterproofing market, with Damp Proof called the company's single largest product.

parts.name: Projects / B2B business
parts.what: Selling directly to builders, large factories, hospitality chains and government infrastructure projects (airports, ports, tunnels, bridges); repeatedly called a strong growth engine, though it slowed in Q4 FY24 when the election code delayed government spending.

parts.name: Industrial coatings and JVs (APPPG and PPGAP with PPG of the U.S.)
parts.what: Coatings for industrial and automotive-type applications run through two joint ventures with PPG; management says it performed strongly for three years running and adds roughly one percentage point to reported growth when included.

parts.name: Home décor — Beautiful Homes stores and services
parts.what: A push from 'share of surface' to 'share of space,' offering kitchen, bath, sanitary, lighting, tiles, flooring and rugs under one roof through about 31 Beautiful Homes stores plus a personalised interior-design service in nine cities, anchored on the beautifulhomes.com digital platform.

parts.name: Kitchen and Bath businesses
parts.what: Modular kitchens and bath fittings — in Q1 FY23 kitchen grew 66% to about Rs. 111 crores and bath grew 116% to about Rs. 119 crores, both crossing the Rs. 100 crore mark in a quarter, with bath turning a small profit and a new Pune plant planned.

parts.name: Acquired décor brands — Weatherseal and White Teak
parts.what: Weatherseal sells UPVC windows and doors and White Teak sells decorative lighting/fans; White Teak was described as a Rs. 20 crore quarterly business against Rs. 57 crores for the whole prior year, so both are small but fast-growing add-ons.

parts.name: Services (Beautiful Homes Painting Service, Total Assure, Smart Assure, Metacare, AP Assure)
parts.what: Paid, supervised painting and asset-care services — a consumer painting service management calls the world's largest, supervision-led services for large projects and waterproofing, and Metacare for maintaining and protecting factory assets against corrosion — positioned as a differentiator no competitor matches.

parts.name: International / AP Global business
parts.what: Paint operations outside India across Asia, the Middle East, Africa and the South Pacific, which delivered double-digit growth in the quarter discussed.

parts.name: Manufacturing and backward integration
parts.what: Its own plants — expanded from about 17 lakh to 22.7 lakh KL a year through brownfield projects at Kasna, Khandala, Ankleshwar and Mysuru, with a 4,00,000 KL greenfield plant in Madhya Pradesh targeted for 2028 — plus a white cement plant in Fujairah to make key raw materials in-house and cut costs.

parts.name: Innovation and patents
parts.what: An in-house R&D engine that management says has produced more than 160 patents, with commercialised launches such as Graphene-based exteriors, the anti-termite 'PU Gold' finish and 'Damp Secure', used to keep products hard for competitors to copy.

overview.what_it_does: ASK Automotive makes and sells auto parts in India, overwhelmingly for two-wheelers (motorcycles and scooters) — its results track two-wheeler production volumes reported by SIAM, and management repeatedly benchmarks growth against that industry. It earns money by supplying components to vehicle makers (OEMs, described as "our prestigious OEMs", including in the fast-growing EV two-wheeler space) and by selling the same kinds of parts as replacement products through a large dealer network in India's independent aftermarket, where a GST cut from 28% to 18% is helping it take share from grey-market and counterfeit sellers. Its three named product segments are Advanced Braking Systems, Aluminium Lightweighting Precision Solutions and Safety Control Cables; consolidated income was about Rs 3,005 crore in FY24, and by FY26 EBITDA was Rs 551 crore at a 13.1% margin with EPS of Rs 15.08. Manufacturing is entirely India-based across multiple plants (Manesar/Haryana head office, plus a large new plant at Karoli in Rajasthan and one in Bangalore serving southern OEMs), with a modest export business of roughly Rs 141-147 crore a year.

parts.name: Advanced Braking System
parts.what: Braking parts such as brake shoes and brake pads for two-wheelers, where management says it holds the market leadership position (roughly 10-12% share in brake pads specifically) and is expanding capacity toward 32 crore brake shoes and pads; revenue grew 7% in FY24, 16% in FY25 and 17% in FY26.

parts.name: Aluminium Lightweighting Precision Solutions
parts.what: Aluminium castings/precision parts that make vehicles lighter and help with thermal management, sold to Indian and global OEMs; this is the fastest-growing of the three segments (up 29% in FY24, 28% in FY25, 30% in FY26) and its profitability swings with aluminium alloy prices, which are passed through to customers.

parts.name: Safety Control Cable
parts.what: Control cables used in vehicles; the smallest of the three named segments by the tone of management commentary, growing 36% in FY24, 14% in FY25 and 14% in FY26.

parts.name: Wheel Assembly business (exited)
parts.what: A low-margin assembly business the company deliberately shrank after asking the customer for two years to move it elsewhere — it cost about Rs 300 crore of FY26 revenue but added roughly 80 basis points to margins, and from 1 April 2026 this revenue is nil.

parts.name: Independent aftermarket (replacement parts)
parts.what: Selling parts to end users through ASK's established dealer network rather than to vehicle makers; it grew 24.7% in FY26 and management sees it gaining further share from grey-market operators and duplicators after the GST rate cut.

parts.name: EV segment
parts.what: Supplying components for electric two-wheelers; revenue was Rs 120 crore in FY24 (up 133%), and management says its share grows in line with an EV industry that is still under 5% of total two-wheeler volumes.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: Overseas sales of the same components, at Rs 147 crore in FY24 and FY25 and Rs 141 crore in FY26 — a small slice that has stalled on tariffs, geopolitical tension and supply-chain and logistics costs, with a Ford order pending.

parts.name: ASK Fras-le joint venture (commercial vehicles)
parts.what: A 49%-owned JV covering the commercial-vehicle business, which turned around from a Rs 6 crore loss share in FY23 to a Rs 16.5 crore profit share in FY24.

parts.name: AISIN joint venture (passenger-car aftermarket)
parts.what: A JV signed in April 2024 with Japan's AISIN, a top-10 global tier-one supplier, in which ASK holds 51%, to market and sell passenger-car components through ASK's independent aftermarket dealer network; the product range was unveiled at Bharat Mobility Global Expo 2025 and launched in April 2025.

parts.name: HPDC alloy wheels (new initiative)
parts.what: A planned two-wheeler alloy-wheel line using high-pressure die casting, with technical tie-ups with LIOHO of Taiwan and Kyushu Yanagawa Seiki of Japan; capacity is built and the product was still under testing as of the FY25 call, positioned as a first-mover advantage versus India's usual gravity die-cast wheels.

parts.name: Captive solar power
parts.what: Not a revenue line but a cost initiative: a 9.9 MW solar plant at Sirsa, Haryana (about Rs 48 crore, fully operational since April 2025) plus a second 11.55 MW plant in Bikaner, Rajasthan due in Q2 FY27, both for the company's own factory consumption.

overview.what_it_does: Aster DM Healthcare runs hospitals and clinics in India, selling medical treatment directly to patients — from routine care to complex, high-end tertiary and quaternary work like cardiology, oncology, robotic surgery and DBS procedures. It makes money by filling beds and treating patients, so revenue tracks patient volumes multiplied by the average realisation per patient (ARPP/ARPOB); bills are paid partly in cash by patients, partly by insurers, and partly under government schemes, with cash and insurance together at about 83% of the combined platform's mix in FY26. Around the hospitals it runs smaller add-on businesses: diagnostic labs, Aster-branded retail pharmacies and patient experience centres, plus an asset-light 'O&M' model where it operates hospitals it doesn't own. It was originally a two-geography group — India plus the GCC (Gulf), which was the larger half at Rs 7,870 crore of Rs 10,250 crore group revenue in FY22 — but the GCC business was sold off/segregated in FY24, leaving a pure India company that is now merging with Quality Care India Ltd to create a roughly 10,620-bed, 28-city, Rs 9,273 crore-revenue pan-India platform.

parts.name: Core hospitals and clinics (India)
parts.what: The main business — multi-specialty hospitals plus attached clinics treating inpatients and outpatients; it is about 94% of India revenue (Rs 968 crore of Rs 1,002 crore in Q1 FY25) and earns the best margins, around 21-23% operating EBITDA, with mature hospitals over six years old carrying most of it.

parts.name: GCC operations (until FY24)
parts.what: Hospitals, clinics and pharmacies across the Gulf, once the bigger half of the group at Rs 7,870 crore revenue and Rs 1,130 crore EBITDA in FY22, which was separated out in a sale that left Aster as an India-only company with cash on hand from the proceeds.

parts.name: Aster Labs (diagnostics)
parts.what: A diagnostics/pathology chain sold alongside the hospitals; small but growing steadily at 15-18% a year and now profitable, at roughly Rs 39 crore of revenue in Q3 FY26 versus Rs 1,186 crore for the company.

parts.name: Pharmacies and patient experience centres
parts.what: Aster-branded retail pharmacy stores and small front-end collection/consult points — 217 pharmacies and 229 patient experience centres as of June 2024 — described as a 'new business' feeding the core network rather than a major profit source.

parts.name: O&M (operations and management) hospitals
parts.what: An asset-light arrangement where Aster runs hospital beds owned by someone else for a fee; a small slice (about Rs 38 crore of Q1 FY25 revenue) but growing fast, up 89% year-on-year, and now EBITDA-positive.

parts.name: Medical Value Travel (MVT)
parts.what: Treating international patients who fly in for care, especially into Kerala from the Middle East and Maldives; a fast-growing, high-value slice with revenue up about 41% year-on-year in FY26.

parts.name: Quality Care India Ltd (merger, pending)
parts.what: A separate hospital group being merged into Aster — shareholders approved it with 96.7% in favour and only final NCLT sanction was pending as of May 2026 — which roughly doubles the platform to Rs 9,273 crore of combined FY26 revenue and Rs 2,013 crore of operating EBITDA, with a pipeline to take beds past 15,000.

overview.what_it_does: Astral is an India-based maker of plastic pipes and fittings for plumbing, drainage, fire-sprinkler and infrastructure use, sold mainly through a dealer/distributor channel and specified by consultants, plumbers and project builders. Around that core piping business it has added related building-products lines — adhesives and construction chemicals, bathware (faucets, sanitaryware, PTMT fittings), water tanks, valves and paints — largely so the same channel and the same brand can carry more products. It makes money by manufacturing at its own plants across India (Santej, Hyderabad, Ghiloth, Kanpur, Rajasthan, Guwahati, Dahej, Jamnagar and others) and selling on volume at managed margins; management repeatedly cites roughly 15%-18% EBITDA margins and, in the more recent calls, double-digit volume growth. Operations are overwhelmingly Indian, plus an adhesives business in the UK (a 100%-owned subsidiary since FY26) with a US manufacturing and sales arm, and some export enquiries for valves.

parts.name: Pipes / Plumbing (piping business)
parts.what: The original and by far the biggest business — CPVC and PVC pipes and fittings for plumbing, plus drainage (Drain Pro, Silencio low-noise), fire-sprinkler CPVC, OPVC, composite pipe and water tanks; it is the anchor of the company (Rs 1,400 crore of capex over ~4 years went across verticals with piping plants central), and grew 15.75% in Q2 FY26 with 20% volume growth company-wide.

parts.name: Infra pipes
parts.what: Large-diameter and specialised pipes for government and infrastructure projects, including double-wall corrugated pipe (a corrugator being added at almost every plant), desalination products and pipe used in projects like the bullet train; described as running at or beyond capacity in 2023 but as a weak, low-government-spending area in FY25-FY26.

parts.name: Valves (ball valve division)
parts.what: A newer in-house line of industrial ball valves, thick ball and non-return valves in PVC and CPVC from 0.5 inch to 4 inch, built with moulds and parts sourced from Europe; still small but expanding, with about 50 SKUs going into commercial production from Q4 FY25.

parts.name: Adhesives India
parts.what: Adhesives, sealants and construction chemicals (from the Resinova acquisition about 13 years ago), run in four sub-segments — maintenance, industrial chemicals, industrial adhesives and wood — plus construction chemicals; it grows steadily at roughly a 15% run rate with 15%-16% EBITDA margins, crossed Rs 100 crore in construction chemicals in FY26, and management's stated ambition is Rs 2,000 crore of Indian revenue within 3-4 years.

parts.name: Adhesives UK (and US)
parts.what: The overseas adhesives arm — a UK business (made a 100% subsidiary, with a new India-based CEO installed after mismanagement) plus a US plant making waterproofing products, adhesives, sealants and silicones that were previously exported from the UK; it was the problem child, swinging from -2% EBITDA in Q2 FY25 to 7.33% in Q2 FY26, with management guiding to 8-10%+ EBITDA and double-digit growth.

parts.name: Bathware (faucets and sanitaryware)
parts.what: Faucets, ceramic sanitaryware and a 150-SKU PTMT taps and bathroom-fittings range, made largely in-house at an expanded Jamnagar plant and sold through the same plumbers, consultants and dealers as pipes; it is a small but fast-growing line off a low base — about Rs 29 crore of net sales in Q2 FY25 (up 63%), 20% growth in H1 FY26, and 25-30% growth in faucets with a large project order book by May 2026.

parts.name: Paints
parts.what: Decorative and industrial paints built on the acquired Gem Paints business, relaunched under the Astral brand and rolled out state by state (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Rajasthan) through newly opened depots; it is the smallest and least mature line — growth was only 4.5% in Q2 FY25 before reaching about 19-20% in FY26 — and margins are still squeezed by the cost of building distribution and manpower.

overview.what_it_does: Astra Microwave Products is a Hyderabad-based electronics maker that has been designing and building RF (radio frequency) and microwave components, subsystems and complete systems for about 30 years, selling mainly into defence, space, meteorology and hydrology. Its customers are largely Indian government-linked buyers — defence PSUs like Bharat Electronics, DRDO labs, the armed forces, ISRO and the India Meteorological Department — plus a smaller export book; it makes money by winning development and production contracts and delivering hardware against them, with orders typically executed over 12-24 months. Revenue was INR 1,157 crores in FY26 with a standalone order book of INR 2,141 crores as of March 2026, of which the December 2025 split was INR 1,477 crores from defence PSUs/DRDO, INR 369 crores metrology and hydrology, INR 249 crores space and INR 130 crores exports/deemed exports. Operations are centred on multiple manufacturing units around Hyderabad, Telangana, plus an R&D centre at Bangalore Aerospace Park, with a joint venture, Astra Rafael Comsys, alongside wholly-owned subsidiaries; management has in-principle approved demerging the space, meteorology and hydrology business into a separate entity.

parts.name: Radar
parts.what: Management calls this the core area — transmit-receive modules for active phased array radars plus subsystems (power amplifiers, receivers, exciters, filters, synthesizers, converters) and full radar systems such as shipborne, coastal surveillance, anti-drone, ground penetration, telemetry, instrumentation and precision approach radars; it is the biggest piece, described as contributing nearly 60% of FY26 revenue and the largest chunk of the order pipeline.

parts.name: Electronic Warfare (EW)
parts.what: Supplies EW subsystems and components — direction-finding receivers, passive homing heads for RF seekers, jammers, filters, amplifiers and wideband receivers — to Indian Air Force, Navy and Army programmes, including a DcPP win for EW suites on the Su-30 platform; sized in early calls at roughly INR 1,000 crores of potential orders over five to six years and a regular second contributor after radar.

parts.name: Missile and Telemetry (guided weapons)
parts.what: Makes telemetry subsystems such as S-band FM transmitters, airborne RF transceivers, ground up/down converters, switch antenna systems and tracking systems, plus guided-weapon work like a terahertz proximity sensor developed with DRDO and subsystems for QRSAM; a smaller line, put at around INR 1,000 crores of five-to-six-year potential together with telemetry.

parts.name: Space
parts.what: Supplies microwave components and subsystems for ground stations and satellite payloads, launch-vehicle microelectronics for private players, and checkout hardware for ISRO's Gaganyaan mission; grew from a small base to over 11% of revenue in Q1 FY25 and INR 249 crores of the December 2025 order book, and is described as a major long-term growth driver.

parts.name: Meteorology and Hydrology
parts.what: Builds wind profile radars, Doppler weather radars and automatic weather stations, largely for IMD, an area where the company says few Indian firms can design and build the equipment; INR 369 crores of the December 2025 order book, and together with space it made up about 16% of FY26 revenue.

parts.name: SATCOM / communications
parts.what: Provides SATCOM and MSS terminals for disaster communication and, more recently, software defined radios (SDR), which management flags as a notable recent order win alongside Doppler weather radars.

parts.name: MMIC and microelectronics
parts.what: In-house chip-level capability for radar and communication systems, held under joint IP rights with DRDO labs, which management describes as a competitive edge and part of a proprietary-product pipeline rather than a separately sized revenue line.

parts.name: Exports and deemed exports
parts.what: Sales outside India, a mix of build-to-print and build-to-spec work; once as high as 39% of revenue in Q1 FY23, it settled around 21% in Q1 FY25 and 12% of the consolidated order book, with INR 130 crores in the December 2025 book.

parts.name: Astra Rafael Comsys (joint venture)
parts.what: A separately reported JV serving PSUs and the Ministry of Defence that closed FY26 with an order book of about INR 625 crores and is expected to deliver over INR 600 crores of revenue in FY27, though FY26 profit was hit by forex-related provisions.

overview.what_it_does: Adani Total Gas Limited (ATGL) is an Indian city gas distribution (CGD) company: it buys natural gas and pipes or dispenses it to end users in the cities and districts it has been licensed to serve. It sells CNG to vehicles through its own network of filling stations (707 stations as of June 2026, plus more via its joint venture) and piped natural gas (PNG) to household kitchens (about 11.4 lakh homes) and to industrial and commercial customers (about 10,400). It makes money on the spread between what it pays for gas — a mix of government-allocated domestic APM/New Well gas, long-term imported contracts and spot LNG purchases — and the calibrated retail price it charges consumers, so margins swing with gas sourcing costs; FY2025-26 revenue was INR6,415 crores with EBITDA of INR1,225 crores. It operates across 53 geographical areas covering roughly 14% of India's population and 125 districts, of which 34 are served directly and 19 through a 50-50 joint venture with IndianOil.

parts.name: CNG (compressed natural gas for transport)
parts.what: Sells CNG as a cheaper vehicle fuel through company-run and dealer-run (CODO/DODO) filling stations — the biggest and fastest-growing part, roughly two-thirds of gas volumes and growing 17-19% a year on the calls.

parts.name: PNG - Domestic (piped natural gas to homes)
parts.what: Pipes gas directly into household kitchens via steel and MDPE pipeline networks, with about 11.4 lakh connections and roughly 137,000 added in FY2025-26; volumes grow more slowly (4-6%) than CNG.

parts.name: PNG - Industrial and Commercial
parts.what: Supplies piped gas as a fuel to factories and commercial establishments (about 10,400 customers directly); management describes this as the segment most exposed to gas supply shortfalls and price swings.

parts.name: Pipeline and station infrastructure
parts.what: Builds and owns the physical network — 15,987-inch km of steel pipeline plus over 8,300 km of MDPE last-mile pipe — which management treats as the backbone that drives all future volume growth.

parts.name: E-mobility / EV charging (ATEL subsidiary)
parts.what: Operates a nationwide EV charging network of 5,306 charge points across 26 states and 226 cities (58 MW installed), targeting 10,000 points; small in revenue terms but growing 100% year-on-year.

parts.name: Biomass / Compressed Bio-Gas (ATBL)
parts.what: Produces and sells CBG from its Barsana plant along with organic manure by-products (FOM/PROM); described on the calls as an emerging, early-stage business.

parts.name: LNG for long-haul mobility (LTM)
parts.what: Sets up LNG fuelling stations for long-distance trucks and buses, starting with a first station at Tirupur, Tamil Nadu — the newest and smallest of the businesses mentioned.

parts.name: IndianOil-Adani Gas Private Limited (IOAGPL) - 50:50 JV
parts.what: A joint venture with IndianOil that runs the CGD business in 19 additional geographical areas, adding roughly 460 CNG stations and lifting the combined network to about 1,167 stations and 13.74 lakh household customers.

overview.what_it_does: Ather Energy makes and sells electric two-wheelers (scooters) in India, under two product lines described on the calls: the original 450 performance range and Rizta, a lower-priced family/convenience scooter launched in FY25 that by Q4 FY26 was about three-quarters of sales. It sells to retail consumers through a dealer-run store network that management doubled from 351 stores in March 2025 to 700 by March 2026, backed by service centres and a company-installed fast-charging network (3,611 chargers as of FY25). Most revenue comes from selling the scooters themselves — 155,000 units and INR 2,305 crores of total income in FY25, rising to roughly INR 940-1,000 crores of income per quarter and 83,000 units in Q4 FY26 — with government EV subsidies forming part of that realisation; a growing slice (14% of revenue in Q3 FY26) is non-vehicle income from software packs, accessories and servicing, which carries higher margins. Operations are almost entirely Indian, split by management into South India (its historic stronghold, ~23-25% market share), 'Middle India' (five states it targeted in FY26, taking share from ~4% to ~17%) and 'Rest of India', plus a small international presence with Sri Lanka added as a second export market; the company is still loss-making but narrowed EBITDA losses from -36% in FY24 to about -3% in Q3 FY26.

parts.name: Rizta (family scooter line)
parts.what: A cheaper, practical family scooter launched in Q2 FY25 that dropped the entry price from about INR 130,000 to INR 109,000; management calls it the single biggest driver of growth, crossing 2 lakh cumulative units by Q3 FY26 and accounting for nearly three-quarters of sales.

parts.name: Ather 450 (performance scooter line)
parts.what: The original, higher-priced performance scooter range that built the brand — especially in South India — and remains the second of the company's two vehicle platforms alongside Rizta.

parts.name: Software / ProPacks (AtherStack)
parts.what: Optional software feature packs sold on top of the scooter — safety, navigation, convenience and ride-assist features — bought by 88% of FY25 customers, contributing over 600 basis points of revenue and described as the largest single component of non-vehicle revenue and a key reason for the company's premium pricing and margins.

parts.name: Non-vehicle revenue (accessories, spares and service)
parts.what: Everything sold besides the scooter itself, including software, the Halo and Halo Bit smart helmets and servicing; it reached 14% of revenue in Q3 FY26 — its highest ever, close to the 15-17% typical of legacy players — and management expects it to compound as the installed fleet ages and service income builds from a still-early base.

parts.name: Distribution network (stores and service centres)
parts.what: The dealer-operated retail footprint that management calls its main growth lever, doubling from 351 to 700 stores in FY26 at roughly 80-90 new stores a quarter with 75% opened by existing dealers, alongside service centres that more than doubled in the year, including higher-standard 'Ather Gold' centres.

parts.name: Charging infrastructure
parts.what: A company-built fast-charging network that added 1,128 chargers in FY25 to reach 3,611 nationally, supporting the scooters rather than being described as a separate revenue stream.

parts.name: Manufacturing and R&D
parts.what: In-house engineering that management credits with a 31% cost reduction over three-and-a-half years and 643 patents filed to date (283 in FY26), plus 'Factory 3.0' being built at AURIC as the company's largest capacity, intended to scale the upcoming EL platform later in FY27.

parts.name: International (Sri Lanka)
parts.what: A second overseas market opened in FY25; the calls mention it only in passing, with no volume or revenue figures given, implying it is very small relative to India.

overview.what_it_does: Atlanta Electricals is an Indian manufacturer of transformers — the large electrical equipment that steps voltage up or down so power can travel across the grid and be used by industry. It sells these units mainly to state and central power utilities (such as Gujarat's GETCO, Rajasthan's RVPNL and Punjab's PSTCL), to private power and renewable-energy developers (Adani Green Energy, Tata Power), and to industrial customers, with a small but newly started export business; management calls itself a "pure-play transformer manufacturer" with over three decades of history and 251 customers across 19 states and three union territories. It makes money by winning tenders and orders, building the transformers to order in its own plants, and dispatching them — revenue is recognised as orders execute, so the order book (INR 3,117 crores as of 30 June 2026) drives future sales, and margins improve as its plants run fuller and as it sells bigger, higher-voltage units. It operates five manufacturing units in India — three legacy plants in Anand (Gujarat) and Bengaluru, plus the newer Vadod plant (Unit 4) and the Atlanta Trafo plant at Ankhi (Unit 5) — with total capacity of 63,060 MVA and seven in-house NABL-accredited testing labs; FY26 revenue was INR 1,851.5 crores with PAT of INR 201.8 crores.

parts.name: Power transformers
parts.what: The core product — large grid transformers ranging from 33 kV class up to 765 kV extra-high-voltage units, which management says accounted for roughly 79% of revenue in Q1 FY27, with 220 kV class alone about 52% of FY26 revenue and over 55% of the order book.

parts.name: Inverter duty transformers
parts.what: Transformers built for solar and other renewable plants (for example a INR 134 crore order from Adani Green Energy), grouped by management with auto transformers and other products in the roughly 21% of revenue outside power transformers; a dedicated new inverter-duty facility is being built out of internal cash.

parts.name: Auto transformers, reactors and special/furnace/generator duty transformers
parts.what: The rest of the six-category product range — including auto transformers (a 220 kV, 150 MVA unit in the GETCO order), 400 kV bus reactors, and furnace, generator and special duty transformers for industrial users — individually small, reported together with inverter duty as the balance of revenue.

parts.name: Transmission & distribution (end market)
parts.what: Supplying state and central transmission utilities, described as the largest end market at about 66% of Q1 FY27 revenue and underpinned by the government's INR 9.6 trillion planned transmission spend through 2032.

parts.name: Renewable energy (end market)
parts.what: Transformers and solar pooling substations for solar and wind projects (INR 116 crores of solar pooling substation orders across Bikaner, Bijapur and Pugal), about 19% of Q1 FY27 revenue.

parts.name: Thermal power and industrial applications (end market)
parts.what: The remaining roughly 15% of revenue, covering thermal generation and assorted industrial customers, which management says adds diversification rather than scale.

parts.name: Atlanta Trafo Private Limited (formerly BTW-Atlanta), Unit 5 at Ankhi
parts.what: A wholly-owned subsidiary acquired in FY26 that brings extra-high-voltage design and testing capability up to 500 MVA / 765 kV; it started production only in Q3 FY26 and produced 580 MVA in FY26, so it is still small but is the platform for the highest-value orders.

parts.name: Vadod plant (Unit 4)
parts.what: The big new 30,000 MVA plant for transformers up to 500 MVA / 400 kV that began production in July 2025, contributed about a third of Q3 FY26 revenue and 6,960 MVA of FY26 output at ~39% of nameplate capacity, and received PGCIL approval for 400 kV manufacturing in April 2026.

parts.name: Exports
parts.what: A newly started activity — management flagged its first significant export order of INR 20 crores in Q3 FY26 as a milestone, so it is currently a very small part of the business.

parts.name: Backward integration (tanks and radiators)
parts.what: An ongoing in-house capex programme, funded from internal cash, to make its own transformer tanks and radiators rather than buy them — aimed at cost and margin rather than being a separate revenue line.

overview.what_it_does: AU Small Finance Bank is an Indian bank, headquartered in Rajasthan and listed in Mumbai (NSE: AUBANK), that started banking operations in April 2017 and lends mostly to small, self-employed borrowers — management says around 80% of its book is informal, self-employed customers who live off business earnings rather than a fixed salary. It takes deposits from retail savers, businesses, government bodies and financial institutions through a branch and touch-point network plus its AU 0101 digital app, and lends that money out as vehicle loans, small-business and home loans against property, gold loans, business/commercial banking loans, microfinance and unsecured credit cards and personal loans. It makes money mainly on the spread between what it pays depositors (cost of funds around 7%) and what it earns on loans (yield on advances around 14%), giving a net interest margin near 5.9-6%, plus fee income from insurance distribution, card interchange, deposit and lending charges, wealth management, foreign exchange and remittances, and treasury. By the June 2026 quarter it held about ₹1.58 lakh crore of deposits with a loan book growing 23% year-on-year, earning roughly ₹796 crore of quarterly profit at a 1.7% return on assets; it has applied to the RBI to convert into a full universal bank.

parts.name: Deposits / liability franchise
parts.what: Takes savings, current and term deposits — ₹1.58 lakh crore as of June 2026, with a 29% CASA ratio — organised into four verticals: branch banking (60% of deposits), government and interbank (21%), financial institutions group (8%) and commercial banking/wholesale (7%).

parts.name: Wheels (vehicle finance)
parts.what: The bank's oldest secured lending line, financing vehicles for small operators and self-employed borrowers; management calls it a core, well-performing secured vertical and is rolling it out into roughly 250 additional touch points inherited from the Fincare merger.

parts.name: MBL (mortgage-backed / small business loans)
parts.what: Secured loans to small businesses against property; a key growth engine alongside Wheels, with disbursements up 18% quarter-on-quarter in Q2 FY25 and now sharing back-end teams with home loans to cut cost.

parts.name: Home loans
parts.what: Housing loans to retail customers, one of the four secured retail verticals management lists as performing well; being merged operationally with the MBL business.

parts.name: Gold loans
parts.what: Small loans against gold jewellery, part of the secured retail book and the first business to go live on the bank's new AI-based loan origination platform in 2026.

parts.name: Secured retail assets (combined)
parts.what: Wheels, MBL, home loans and gold together make up about two-thirds of the loan book; management says they are well collateralised with historically low ultimate losses even when reported bad loans rise temporarily.

parts.name: Commercial banking / business banking
parts.what: Lending and transaction services to businesses, including cash management, trade and FX; around 20% of the loan book, with the agri business folded into it in 2026.

parts.name: Microfinance (MFI)
parts.what: Very small group loans to rural borrowers — about 7% of the book with an average outstanding of roughly ₹26,000 per loan across 61,000 villages — a cyclical business that saw sharply higher bad debts in FY25 before recovering by FY26.

parts.name: Credit cards and personal loans (unsecured, digital)
parts.what: Digitally underwritten unsecured lending; growth was deliberately slowed in FY25 on rising credit costs and returned to growth by FY26, with card interchange and fees adding to non-interest income.

parts.name: Fee and other income
parts.what: Non-lending earnings from distributing insurance for about 14 partners, deposit and loan fees, card interchange, wealth management, authorised-dealer (foreign exchange) and remittance services, PSLC sales and treasury — running at roughly a third of net interest income and growing 33% year-on-year in the June 2026 quarter.

parts.name: Digital banking and AI platform (AU 0101)
parts.what: The bank's app and technology stack, now handling over 90% of transactions and service requests, with an agentic-AI platform being used to rebuild loan origination, customer service voice bots in 11 languages, and analytics-driven credit and collections.

overview.what_it_does: Aurionpro Solutions is an India-headquartered technology company that builds and sells its own software products and platforms — plus, in some cases, the hardware and systems around them — mainly to banks and financial institutions, and to transit authorities, governments and data-centre operators. It makes money by winning project-based contracts (licences, implementation and build-out work) that it books into an order book, followed by ongoing maintenance and support contracts that are not counted in that order book; it spends about 9-10% of revenue on R&D to keep the products proprietary. Revenue is reported in two segments, Banking & Fintech and the Technology Innovation Group (TIG), which were roughly the same size in the first nine months of FY26 (TIG Rs.471 crore out of Rs.1,066 crore total, both growing 26%). It sells in India and internationally — the US, Central and Latin America, Africa, Australia, the UK, Singapore and the Middle East — with FY26 revenue of Rs.1,411 crore (up 20.2%), a 20% EBITDA margin, a 15% PAT margin and an order book above Rs.1,800 crore entering FY27.

parts.name: Banking and Fintech
parts.what: Sells software platforms that banks run their core operations on — lending, transaction banking, cash management, trade finance — and was roughly Rs.595 crore of the Rs.1,066 crore nine-month FY26 revenue, growing 26%, with the Middle East described as an increasingly important growth engine (and the source of the FY26 shortfall when war there delayed deals).

parts.name: Lending (Integro)
parts.what: Loan origination, collateral management and limits management software — the calls note Aurionpro was placed in the leaders quadrant of Chartis's RiskTech rankings in all three categories, and won a large lending-modernisation mandate from a Singapore-headquartered bank across its international subsidiaries.

parts.name: Transaction banking / cash management (iCash pro)
parts.what: The platform banks use to run corporate cash-management and transaction-banking services; management says a marquee Indian public sector bank picking it has made it close to the market standard for new deals, with CSB Bank also signing on.

parts.name: Enterprise AI (Arya.AI, Lexsi Labs, AurionAI)
parts.what: An acquired-and-built AI arm making AI products for banks and insurers — including a domain-specific enterprise AI platform, an AI-native agentic trade finance application and in-house foundation models — described as the focus of a heavy, concentrated investment cycle rather than a large revenue line today.

parts.name: Technology Innovation Group (TIG)
parts.what: The non-banking half of the company, made up of three slices — smart mobility/transit payments, data centres, and smart cities — at Rs.471 crore in the first nine months of FY26, up 26%, and historically the larger share of the order book (about 65% versus 35% for banking in 2024).

parts.name: Smart Mobility / transit payments
parts.what: Supplies the fare-collection and related systems that metros and transit agencies use — automated fare collection for Delhi Metro's Bhopal and Indore projects, platform screen doors via Titagarh for Mumbai Metro Line 5, plus wins in the US (including a State of California tender), Latin America, Africa, Australia and the UK, and partnerships with Mastercard and Vix; management says it competes by owning the full stack of software, systems and hardware.

parts.name: Data centres
parts.what: Designs and builds data centres as a single-window provider — including complex jobs like high-performance computing for IIT Guwahati and IIT Bombay, a tier-four design for the RBI, and a project for IDBI Bank — a business that grew over 50% a year for three years and in FY26 landed one of India's largest AI-focused data centre mandates from a hyperscaler, which requires heavy upfront investment and working capital.

parts.name: Smart cities
parts.what: The original third leg of TIG, serving government institutions, but deliberately slowed down by management as a planned de-emphasis rather than a growth driver.

parts.name: Payments (AuroPay)
parts.what: An RBI-authorised online payment aggregator used to bundle payments with Aurionpro's own software — transit fares, lending, SME SaaS — rather than compete as a plain commodity consumer gateway; a newer business that has absorbed meaningful capitalised investment.

overview.what_it_does: Aurobindo Pharma is an India-based (Hyderabad) drug maker that mostly sells generic medicines — copies of drugs whose patents have expired — in pill/oral form, as injectables, and in other formats, plus the bulk chemical ingredients (APIs) that go into medicines. Its customers are overseas buyers first: the US is its single biggest market (about $1.6 billion of sales in FY26), followed by Europe (which crossed €1 billion in FY26), then a set of 'growth markets' such as Canada and India, and government/donor-funded antiretroviral (HIV) tender business. It makes money by manufacturing at large scale in its own plants and getting products approved with regulators (it had filed 838 ANDAs with the US FDA by mid-2024, ~668 approved), then competing largely on volume and reliable supply while prices in generics steadily erode. Group revenue was Rs. 33,653 crores in FY26 with an EBITDA margin of about 20.4%, and management is also spending on newer areas — biosimilars, peptides, vaccines, a China plant, and backward integration into antibiotic raw materials (Pen-G).

parts.name: Formulation business
parts.what: The finished-medicine business (tablets, capsules, injectables) sold across the US, Europe, growth markets and ARV; it is the bulk of the company at roughly 86-89% of total revenue, Rs. 7,646 crores in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: API business
parts.what: Sells the active pharmaceutical ingredients — the bulk chemicals inside drugs — to other manufacturers and to its own plants; smaller but steady at roughly 11-14% of revenue, about Rs. 4,047 crores for full-year FY26.

parts.name: US formulations (Aurobindo Pharma USA)
parts.what: The oral-solid generics business in the United States, described as a large, diversified portfolio that keeps pricing stable; US revenue was $387 million in Q4 FY26 and $1,631 million for the full year, with management aiming at $2 billion 'over the near term'.

parts.name: Injectables and specialty (Eugia Pharma Specialities / AuroMedics)
parts.what: A separately-run unit making injectable and specialty products, treated as a higher-value growth engine; global specialty and injectable revenue was $513 million in FY26, growing 12-13% year-on-year excluding gRevlimid.

parts.name: Europe formulations business
parts.what: Generic formulations sold across key European markets, called a 'strategic growth engine' and the fastest grower recently at ~27-30% year-on-year; it hit the €1 billion annual revenue milestone in FY26.

parts.name: Growth markets
parts.what: Everything outside the US and Europe — Canada, India and other newer geographies — worth Rs. 3,499 crores (about $397 million) in FY26, expanded through launches and bolt-on acquisitions such as Khandelwal Laboratories' non-oncology business.

parts.name: ARV formulation business
parts.what: Antiretroviral (HIV) medicines sold largely through tenders and donor programmes; a smaller line at Rs. 1,384 crores (about $157 million) in FY26, up 33% on tender wins and volumes.

parts.name: Biosimilars, vaccines and peptides
parts.what: A newer R&D-heavy unit under its own CEO developing biologic copies and complex products, still pre-scale — described as 'progressing well' with clinical trials advancing and framed as a long-term growth driver alongside the core generics business.

parts.name: Pen-G / 6APA / Amoxicillin (antibiotic raw materials, PLI project)
parts.what: A large new Indian plant making penicillin and related antibiotic building blocks in-house instead of importing them, ramping toward 10,000+ tonnes a year and expected to lift margins over time, helped by a government minimum-import-price rule.

parts.name: US manufacturing and acquisitions (Dayton, Raleigh, Lannett, Acrotech)
parts.what: Owned US plants for oral, transdermal and respiratory products plus acquired businesses; Dayton has just gone commercial and is expected to contribute meaningfully from FY27, with Lannett still pending regulatory approval.

parts.name: China OSD facility
parts.what: An oral-solid-dosage plant in China building toward 2 billion units a year, supplying mainly Europe and local approvals; still small and only expected to reach EBITDA break-even around Q4 FY26.

overview.what_it_does: Avalon Technologies is an Indian electronics manufacturing services (EMS) company — it does not sell its own branded products, but builds electronic and engineered products under contract for other companies. Its pitch is "high-mix, flexible-volume" work: complex, mission-critical, low-to-medium-volume products with heavy engineering content, rather than cheap mass-market goods. Because it is vertically integrated (PCB design, circuit-board assembly, cables, sheet metal, magnetics, plastics, testing and logistics all in-house), it can deliver a finished "box build" product rather than just a component — box build was 56% of revenue in Q4 FY26, up from 44% four years earlier. It runs 13+ plants in India and the United States, serving customers in rail, aerospace, industrial, clean energy, medical and communications; FY26 revenue was INR1,603 crores (up 46%), with 62% of revenue from US customers and 38% from India, while 77% of manufacturing is done in India.

parts.name: India manufacturing operations
parts.what: The core plants (largely Chennai/Bengaluru) that build for both Indian and global customers — about 77-78% of total revenue and where nearly all the profit sits, at roughly 16.7% EBITDA margin and 12% PAT margin in FY26.

parts.name: US manufacturing operations
parts.what: Plants in the United States serving American customers, about 22-23% of revenue; it has been loss-making (a INR14.2 crore loss in Q1 FY25, narrowed to about INR5 crores in Q4 FY26), and management has shifted 45-50% of that production to India while targeting breakeven in late FY27.

parts.name: Box build (vertically integrated end-product assembly)
parts.what: The flagship offering — taking a customer's product from PCB design through to a fully assembled, tested and shipped finished unit; management calls this its main differentiator and it has grown from 44% of revenue four years ago to 56% in Q4 FY26.

parts.name: PCB design and assembly
parts.what: Design and analysis of printed circuit boards (one of India's largest such teams, based in Bengaluru) plus manufacture of complex multi-layer board assemblies for mission-critical uses like railway signalling, vehicle tracking and medical equipment.

parts.name: Cable assemblies and wire harnesses
parts.what: Complex cabling and harness manufacturing feeding into box builds; management says it is on the cusp of winning cable work with a major aerospace customer, an area of growing interest.

parts.name: Sheet metal and precision machining
parts.what: Precision-engineered metal parts and enclosures for mission-critical applications, carrying NADCAP approval for fabrication and welding — the base for newer bids in aerospace cockpit assemblies and landing gear components.

parts.name: Magnetics
parts.what: Custom-designed transformers of various types, made largely for clean energy and similar products.

parts.name: Plastics
parts.what: A small but growing injection-moulding division that supplies plastic parts into the integrated box-build offering.

parts.name: Industrial vertical
parts.what: The largest end-market at roughly 34-35% of FY26 revenue, growing about 65% year-on-year, covering established industrial equipment makers plus newer wins like semiconductor manufacturing equipment and power systems.

parts.name: Mobility (rail and aerospace)
parts.what: About 28% of FY26 revenue growing ~50%, split between rail at 16% (signalling, locomotive engine subsystems, the Kavach anti-collision system) and aerospace at 9% (cabin subassemblies, work for a large aerospace conglomerate including a factory transfer to India).

parts.name: Clean energy
parts.what: Around 20% of FY26 revenue growing ~45%, covering solar, hydrogen, EV and especially energy storage systems — including a US customer's home electrification/storage-and-grid product now ramping in production.

parts.name: Communications
parts.what: About 8% of FY26 revenue growing ~58%, including control units for satellite antenna systems where prototypes are done and volume orders are expected from FY27.

parts.name: Order book and long-term contracts
parts.what: Firm purchase orders stood at INR2,196 crores as of March 2026 (up ~25%, executed over about 14 months on average), plus a separate INR1,245 crores of longer-term contracts running 15-36 months — the visibility behind management's guidance of 24-27% growth in FY27 and roughly INR3,200 crores of revenue by FY29.
